doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Editing, releasing and promoting the Dream Band records
summary: Dick Bach edited the tapes into a hit release; Gibbs phoned disc jockeys himself, and the CDs sold across Europe.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: want that cut out. He said, “Let me show you. Let me do something for you. Don’t listen to those things at all anymore,” which I hardly ever did because they were on reel to reel. And he cut it to where we made it into a five minute thing where it was almost like it started out, the ensemble, it was an ensemble. Because that was what made the band. Even though we had the greatest soloists, there was the fire of the ensemble, because they played so well together. I mean you find a lot of bands playing but not everybody thought like we did. If you took each guy out in the band on the street and said, “Who is your favorite alto player, who’s your favorite trumpet player, favorite piano player?” Same names. Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Bud Powell. That was our idols. So because of loving the same people, we all felt the same way about the music. So Dick Bach anyway did that, and I did miss the rest of the choruses but he really knew how to cut it. He cut it great. So I agreed to do that. And all I got was $2,500. I paid all the guys myself to put it out. But I did have the use Fantasy, and I made very good friends with Ralph Kaffel later on, the president of Fantasy, who is one of my close friends now. He gave me the use of the Fantasy telephone, their number, to charge every phone call to make sure I can call every disc jockey in the world and charge it to them and make sure, if they don’t have a CD they’ll get one immediately. So I used to get up at 6:00 in the morning. First of all, what happened is when the record first came out we had two radio stations in California, two jazz stations. I’d put on one and all of a sudden I’d hear five of the songs. Then I’d put on the other one and I’d hear four or five more. It became the biggest hit. In California they were playing it, but I didn’t know they were playing it all over. But I would call every disc jockey, and if they didn’t have one — I’d have to get up at 6:00 in the morning in California, because here it’s 9:00 on the west coast. In Europe it’s another time. So sometimes I’d be sitting there at 6:00 in the morning in my underwear and it would be like 8:00 at night and I’m still sitting there, hadn’t had anything to eat. On the phone. Because I didn’t believe what was happening. And the band made a success all over the world. To a point where when Buddy and I went to Europe this last time, we did about sixteen, seventeen one nighters in England, and the promoter brought our CDs that Buddy and I did to sell. And the Europeans, they are very brave, they just walk in your dressing room, they just walk in, didn’t even knock on the door, walk in, to sign autographs. And not only did they come with the Buddy DeFranco Terry Gibbs album, but every little town, everybody would have all five CDs of the Dream Band. At least four or five guys in every town. I never knew it got out that far. And it really made that much noise. Now they are being sold, copies of the original arrangements. No new copies are being made of the things that Joe Maini marked in and what Mel Lewis marked in. Just like they was, they’re being sold. Dave Pell, who has the octet, he distributes them for me. © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-
